title: Assessment of PFAS toxicity using lux-marked bioluminescent Pseudomonas biosensors
content:
Abstract
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent fluorinated contaminants of growing environmental concern, yet rapid methods for assessing their biological effects remain limited. This study evaluated lux-marked Pseudomonas putida F1 Tn5 luxCDABE and P. putida 12708 Tn5 luxCDABE as whole-cell biosensors for detecting sublethal PFAS toxicity. Fluoride bioassays confirmed both strains tolerated up to 1,000 mg L−1 fluoride without measurable bioluminescence inhibition, supporting their suitability for PFAS exposure studies. Growth and bioluminescence responses were then assessed in M9 minimal medium following exposure to PFOA, PFNA, and PFHxS. Conventional growth measurements showed limited effects across tested concentrations, with strain-specific reductions observed mainly in P. putida F1 Tn5 luxCDABE. Bioluminescence revealed clearer compound- and concentration-dependent responses. PFOA and PFNA caused significant inhibition of peak bioluminescence in P. putida F1 Tn5 luxCDABE, while P. putida 12708 Tn5 luxCDABE showed a variable response, including increased luminescence following PFOA exposure and inhibition at higher concentrations of selected PFAS. These findings demonstrate that lux-marked P. putida biosensors are able to detect PFAS-induced metabolic stress with greater sensitivity than conventional growth assays and highlights their potential as rapid tools for ecotoxicological screening of fluorinated contaminants.

title: Tree island area in oil palm agroforests directly and indirectly drives evaporative fraction
content:
Tree island area in oil palm agroforests directly and indirectly drives evaporative fraction
Thorge Wintz, Alexander Röll, Gustavo Brant Paterno, Florian Ellsäßer, Delphine Clara Zemp, Hendrayanto, Bambang Irawan, Alexander Knohl, Holger Kreft, and Dirk Hölscher
Biogeosciences, 23, 7643–7660, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-7643-2026, 2026
We investigated how the size and diversity of tree patches in Indonesian oil palm landscapes influence the movement of water to the atmosphere and local cooling. Our study shows that larger tree patches increase cooling mainly by supporting greater plant diversity and more complex vegetation structure. These findings suggest that expanding and diversifying tree patches can help manage microclimate and water cycling in agricultural areas.

title: Nitrous oxide dynamics across nitrogen and pH gradients in headwater streams
content:
Nitrous oxide dynamics across nitrogen and pH gradients in headwater streams
Mette V. Carstensen, Annelies J. Veraart, Ida F. Peterse, Nicole Wrage-Mönnig, and Joachim Audet
Biogeosciences, 23, 7661–7677, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-7661-2026, 2026
We studied seventy-two small streams to understand why some release more nitrous oxide, a powerful greenhouse gas, than others. By measuring water chemistry and physical factors across seasons, we found a strong positive association between nitrate and nitrous oxide levels, especially in acidic waters. Overall, these results show that managing nitrogen in sensitive landscapes might reduce climate impacts.

title: The open uncertainty window in ocean biogeochemical responses to fossil carbon emissions
content:
The open uncertainty window in ocean biogeochemical responses to fossil carbon emissions
Karin Kvale, Ivy Frenger, Julia Getzlaff, Wolfgang Koeve, Iris Kriest, Angela Landolfi, and Andreas Oschlies
Biogeosciences, 23, 7679–7704, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-7679-2026, 2026
We tried to understand how parameter choices can impact ocean model results over long-timescale simulations. Using a standard ocean biogeochemical model, we modified the physics slightly and then used an objective tuning procedure to create 3 ocean biogeochemical models that perform nearly identically for the modern ocean. These 3 models gave similar results but for different underlying reasons, which caused the models to respond differently when forced with fossil CO2 emissions.

title: Contrasting Controls on Air–Sea CO2 Fluxes in the Pearl River Estuary and Adjacent Coastal Waters Under Typhoon Intensification and Track Shifts: A Modeling Study
content:
Abstract
Northwest Pacific typhoons frequently affect the northern South China Sea, but their impacts on air‐sea CO2 flux (FCO2) in the Pearl River Estuary (PRE) and adjacent coastal waters remain poorly constrained. We used a coupled physical‐biogeochemical model to simulate Typhoon Hato (2017) and conducted sensitivity experiments with intensified winds and northward‐shifted tracks to quantify their effects on FCO2 variability. Hato converted both regions into pronounced CO2 sources, with mean estuarine FCO2 increasing ∼15× relative to pre‐typhoon conditions. During the event, FCO2 variability was governed primarily by air‐sea partial pressure difference of CO2 (ΔpCO2); in coastal waters it arose mainly from vertical mixing of DIC, whereas in the estuary it reflected TA advection. Wind‐intensification experiments showed that FCO2 increased nonlinearly with wind speed. In coastal waters, the drivers of FCO2 anomaly (ΔFCO2) shifted toward a dominance of the gas transfer velocity (k), whereas estuarine anomalies remained jointly controlled by gas transfer velocity and non‐thermal pCO2 (pCO2_noSST); sea surface temperature (SST) effects remained secondary. Track‐shift experiments redistributed process importance. In coastal waters, the contribution from the gas transfer (k) term declined and enhanced pCO2_noSST moderated ΔFCO2 peaks, whereas in the estuary an increased SST contribution and reduced k‐term contribution amplified peak variability. This paper shows that extreme typhoons trigger brief, intense nearshore CO2 outgassing pulses, and that future intensity increased and track shifts may reshape FCO2 magnitude and controls, increasing coastal carbon‐budget uncertainty.

title: Riverine and Submarine Groundwater Discharge Jointly Shape Dissolved Black Carbon Budgets in the Northern Beibu Gulf
content:
Abstract
Dissolved black carbon (DBC) is a major refractory component of marine dissolved organic carbon, yet its sources and transport pathways in coastal systems remain incompletely constrained. Here, we investigate the seasonal dynamics of DBC in the northern Beibu Gulf, a monsoon‐influenced marginal sea. DBC concentrations (0.7–2.4 μmol L−1) showed strong negative correlations with salinity, indicating that freshwater‐seawater mixing is a dominant control on DBC distributions. Riverine DBC concentrations of the major rivers were reconstructed using a254‐based relationships, yielding a discharge‐weighted riverine DBC endmember of ∼10 μmol L−1 (95% bootstrap confidence interval (CI): 9.2–10.9 μmol L−1) in the wet season. This value accounted for most of the wet‐season effective DBC (DBCeff) derived from the DBC–salinity relationship (∼11.9 μmol L−1; 95% CI: 10.3–13.7 μmol L−1), with a difference of 1.9 μmol L−1 (95% CI: 0.09–3.8 μmol L−1), reflecting potential non‐riverine contributions. Wet‐season flux estimates indicate that riverine discharge contributes ∼8.0 t day−1 of DBC, whereas non‐riverine sources, primarily submarine groundwater discharge (SGD), contribute ∼1.7 t day−1, highlighting the contribution of non‐riverine pathways to coastal DBC transport. Compared with the dry season, the wet season had higher DBC concentrations and DBCeff, reflecting stronger terrestrial influence. Furthermore, DBC concentrations were lower in surface than bottom waters at similar salinities in the wet season, potentially due to photodegradation and sedimentary inputs. These results highlight the dominant role of rivers in transporting DBC to coastal seas while demonstrating the need to incorporate SGD and other coastal pathways into regional carbon budgets.

title: Evaluating Recent Trends in Mixed Layer Depth Around the Kerguelen Plateau
content:
Abstract
The Kerguelen Plateau in the Southern Indian Ocean sustains intense phytoplankton blooms through local iron enrichment. Changes in mixed‐layer depth (MLD) can therefore affect regional ecosystem functioning and air–sea carbon exchange. Using 17 years (2007–2023) of observations from animal‐borne sensors and Argo floats, we reconstruct monthly MLD from sparse in situ data using principal components analysis through conditional expectation (PACE). The method is evaluated using GLORYS and a masked version reproducing the observational sampling pattern. The reconstruction captures the dominant seasonal cycle and leading spatial pattern of MLD variability. The masked‐reanalysis experiment shows that broad interannual fluctuations are more stable than fitted trends, which are particularly sampling‐sensitive. We examine these trends to determine whether the observational record supports sustained MLD change or instead reflects sampling‐induced variability. We find a deeper‐MLD region over and west of the Kerguelen Plateau, surrounded by a shallower‐MLD region and bounded to the north by the deep mixing band. Observation‐based trend estimates for 2007–2023 indicate a weak summer deepening tendency of about 0.2myr−1 $0.2\hspace*{.5em}\mathrm{m}\hspace*{.5em}\mathrm{y}{\mathrm{r}}^{-\mathrm{1}}$, consistent with GLORYS but not statistically significant. A winter shallowing tendency is obtained from the sparse reconstructions; however, it is mostly a result of poor data sampling. In the early 1990s, bottle profiles from the KERFIX station give deeper MLD than at the nearest grid point in 2007–2023, in winter and summer, but this contrast is difficult to interpret as a long‐term trend. Overall, the results suggest that domain‐wide MLD has not changed significantly around the Kerguelen region in the last two decades.

title: Linking Population Genomics and Movement Ecology for Shark Conservation
content:
ABSTRACT
Climate change and overexploitation are increasingly threatening sharks, with pelagic species among the most affected. The complex ecology and life histories of these species, however, pose major challenges for conservation planning. Here, we examine how integrating genomics and movement ecology can better inform the conservation of highly migratory sharks. The growing availability of reference genomes and expanding population genomic datasets in sharks, coupled with advances in biologging, creates unprecedented opportunities to integrate these approaches and link long‐term, population‐level evolutionary processes with short‐term individual, behavioural patterns. This mini review explores research applications that integrate both fields to overcome their individual limitations and strengthen the evidence and conclusions used to inform conservation. Then we discuss, based on previous studies, how this framework can address specific conservation objectives and lead to decision‐ready outcomes, including the delineation of management units, the design of spatial and stock‐specific fisheries management measures, and the assessment of species' vulnerability to climate change. We conclude by highlighting that the translation of this knowledge into practice requires engagement with the scientific and management bodies responsible for evaluating the evidence, advising decision‐makers, and implementing shark conservation measures.

title: Issue Information
Biotic and abiotic factors directly and indirectly shape mixed‐species group structure across a rainfall gradient
content:
Abstract
Mixed‐species animal groups are dynamic systems whose structure and functioning is contingent on biotic (e.g., food acquisition) and abiotic (e.g., climatic conditions) processes. Understanding the interactions among such factors, and the temporal scales at which they operate, can help to understand the mechanisms driving community structure and anticipate the consequences of human‐driven alterations in ecosystem functioning. We used network analyses and Bayesian causal inference to study how direct and indirect effects of biotic and abiotic factors affected the structure of mixed‐species groups of army ant–following birds (a bird aggregation specialized on feeding at army ant swarms). Our study revealed that the structure of interactions among birds visiting ant swarms was modulated by short‐term rainfall, swarm traits, and the food resources they provide. Specifically, we found that ant‐follower groups had 29% to 54.7% more species when swarms were larger, provided higher food resources, and the environment experienced high precipitation during the previous 15 days. Similarly, the ant‐follower groups were 34% more cohesive (i.e., a tendency toward the formation of densely connected subgroups), attendant birds interacted with 55% more partners, and interactions in the groups were more evenly distributed among partners in swarms with high food resources. Our data suggest that rainfall effects have the potential to propagate through swarm size and food availability to affect the structure of ant‐followers, but direct effects still occupy the primary role. Notably, the effects of biotic and abiotic predictors were contingent on the season and location along a rainfall gradient. Our study highlights three key points: (1) the factors modulating the structure of mixed‐species animal groups are interlinked, with both abiotic and biotic factors influencing structure; (2) the effect of short‐term rainfall is only detected at particular lagged time windows; and (3) the processes explaining the structure of mixed‐species groups are strongly influenced by seasonality and location along a rainfall gradient. Our study emphasizes the importance of evaluating interdependent relationships between biotic and abiotic processes, their direct and indirect effects on interacting species, appropriate temporal scales, and the consequences of climatic cycles in understanding the mechanisms influencing the structure of mixed‐species groups.

title: ATP-independent entropy-driven dsRNA unwinding by DDX3X revealed by coarse-grained simulations and deep learning
content:
by Kang Wang, Chun-Lai Ren, Yu-Qiang Ma

DEAD-box RNA helicases (DDXs) are traditionally known as ATP-dependent motors that unwind double-stranded RNA (dsRNA). Recent experiments, however, show that some DDXs promote dsRNA unwinding even in the absence of ATP, raising a fundamental question about the physical mechanism underlying ATP-independent strand separation. Here, we develop a minimal, physics-based coarse-grained RNA model and incorporate weak, specific interactions between DDX3X and dsRNA, revealing the inherently stochastic nature of unwinding events. The unwinding process must overcome an energy barrier, but thermal fluctuations and entropy gain provide a driving force for RNA remodeling. We identify that dsRNA separation proceeds through rare yet obligatory strand-displacing intermediates facilitated by DDX3X. By combining deep learning-assisted analysis, we further rank the contributions of different entropic components, revealing hydrogen bonding as the dominant factor, followed by base stacking and then the backbone conformation. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized physical mechanism for RNA duplex unwinding and offer an effective framework for studying RNA remodeling kinetics.

title: Coupled beta and high-frequency oscillations emerge from synchronized bursting in a minimal model of the parkinsonian subthalamic nucleus
content:
by Hiba Sheheitli, Luke A. Johnson, Jing Wang, Joshua E. Aman, Jerrold L. Vitek

Local field potentials (LFPs) recorded from the subthalamic nucleus (STN) in Parkinson's disease (PD) exhibit a distinctive multiscale spectral signature: exaggerated beta-band oscillations (13–30 Hz) coupled to high-frequency oscillations (HFOs, 200–400 Hz), with HFO amplitude being phase-locked to the beta cycle. This phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) has been identified as a promising biomarker of the parkinsonian state, yet no biophysical model has explained how it emerges, what determines the HFO frequency, or how HFOs can exist without beta modulation in the medicated STN. Here we show that a heterogeneous population of excitatory Izhikevich neurons with recurrent coupling produces three dynamical regimes: (i) asynchronous tonic firing, (ii) asynchronous bursting, in which neurons burst individually producing broadband HFO power but without coherent population-level PAC, and (iii) synchronous bursting, which gives rise to beta-HFO PAC. The regimes are governed by two biophysically interpretable parameters that capture complementary effects of dopamine depletion: one reflecting changes in intrinsic neuronal excitability, the other reflecting changes in synaptic coupling strength. The transition from asynchronous to synchronous bursting in this model emulates the emergence of pathological STN neuronal activity in the parkinsonian state. HFO peak frequency varies continuously across the two-parameter landscape, suggesting a possible mechanism of the clinically observed shift from slow (200–300 Hz) to fast (300–400 Hz) HFOs between medication states. The character of the synchronization transition depends on baseline excitability, ranging from a sharp co-emergence of bursting and synchrony at low excitability to a decoupled transition at intermediate excitability, where the bursting fraction saturates while the population synchronization continues to increase with coupling. The asynchronous-to-synchronous bursting transition and the beta-HFO PAC in the STN population also arise in an extended version of the model with reciprocal coupling to an inhibitory population of globus pallidus externa (GPe)-like neurons, with the beta frequency varying with the delay in the synaptic coupling between the two populations. The model generates testable predictions for future clinical and experimental studies, provides a numerical dissection of how mesoscopic LFP features could map onto microscopic neuronal dynamics, and serves as a computational building block for future circuit-level models that may inform brain stimulation strategies tailored to the patient-specific dynamical state of the STN.

title: Ten simple rules for teaching practical AI to health data teams
content:
by Eric Just, Aik Choon Tan

Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly entered the healthcare discourse, often framed through the lens of frontier models, generative systems, and transformative potential. Yet for many healthcare data teams, the practical path from curiosity to capability remains unclear. Concerns about data privacy, regulatory compliance, brittle systems, and misaligned expectations frequently stall progress before meaningful experimentation can begin. This paper presents ten simple rules for teaching practical AI to healthcare data teams, grounded in real-world data, privacy-first experimentation, and system-level thinking. Drawing on hands-on training experiences and existing educational and methodological literature, we argue that AI education in healthcare must prioritize workflows over models, systems over components, and institutional capability over isolated technical success. These rules are intended to help educators and organizational leaders move teams beyond the AI hype cycle toward building trustworthy, sustainable, and context-aware AI systems that matter.

title: Interpretable embeddings of speech explain and enhance the brain encoding performance of audio models
content:
by Riki Shimizu, Richard J. Antonello, Chandan Singh, Nima Mesgarani

Speech foundation models (SFMs) are increasingly hailed as powerful computational models of human speech perception. However, since their representations are inherently black-box, it remains unclear what drives their alignment with brain responses. To remedy this, we built linear encoding models from six interpretable feature families: mel-spectrogram, Gabor filter bank features, speech presence, phonetic, syntactic, and semantic features, and contextualized embeddings from three state-of-the-art SFMs (Whisper, HuBERT, WavLM), quantifying electrocorticography (ECoG) response variance shared between feature classes. Variance-partitioning analyses revealed several key insights: First, the SFMs’ alignment with the brain can be mostly accounted for by their ability to learn and encode simple interpretable speech features. Second, SFMs exhibit a systematic trade-off between encoding of brain-relevant low-level and high-level features across layers. Finally, our results show that SFMs learn brain-relevant semantics which cannot be accounted for by lower-level speech features, with this capacity increasing with model size and context length. Together, our findings suggest a principled approach to build more interpretable, accurate, and efficient encoding models of the brain by augmenting SFM embeddings with interpretable features.

title: Degeneracy in neuronal bifurcation landscapes: Equivalent bifurcation sequences across distinct parameter sets
content:
by Gianmarco Cafaro, Christophe Bernard, Meysam Hashemi, Damien Depannemaecker

Degeneracy, the capacity of structurally distinct systems to achieve similar functions, is a fundamental property of living organisms, enabling adaptability and resilience. Neurons can maintain stable activity patterns despite substantial variability in ion channel expression, highlighting how different intrinsic configurations can produce equivalent electrophysiological behaviors. Previous studies have shown that neuronal activity emerges from the interaction between intrinsic membrane properties and ionic concentration dynamics. However, how degeneracy is organized within the dynamical landscape of neurons and how different degenerate configurations respond to external perturbations remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate how distinct biophysical parameter sets generate equivalent bifurcation sequences and how their resilience changes under ionic modulation. Using a minimal neuron model with three variable conductances, we systematically explore how variations in extracellular potassium concentration, representing physiological and pathological conditions, reshape neuronal dynamics. We show that distinct conductance configurations occupy structured regions of parameter space that support the same bifurcation pathways, leading to equivalent activity regimes such as bursting, seizure-like activity, and depolarization block. However, these degenerate configurations exhibit different sensitivities to extracellular perturbations, revealing that functional equivalence under fixed conditions does not imply equivalent robustness. To quantify this effect, we introduce resilience as a measure of the threshold at which a given conductance configuration transitions into a specific activity regime under external ionic changes. Our results demonstrate that degeneracy extends beyond the coexistence of multiple solutions: degenerate configurations form structured landscapes with distinct trajectories under environmental modulation. This framework provides a quantitative approach to investigate how intrinsic variability influences neuronal vulnerability and resilience across different dynamical states.

title: How early microbial encounters shape adult behavior
content:
by Kyu-Chan Cho, Won-Jae Lee

Microbes are increasingly recognized as modulators of host behavior, but the underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. A new PLOS Biology study reveals a microbiome-to-gut-to-neuron pathway linking developmental microbial exposure to later food avoidance. Microbes are increasingly recognized as modulators of host behavior, but the underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. This Primer discusses a new PLOS Biology study that reveals a microbiome-to-gut-to-neuron pathway linking developmental microbial exposure to later food avoidance.

title: Rethinking neurodegeneration: Placing disease in its physiological context
content:
by Joanna Clarke, Sarah Jäkel

Research into neurodegeneration is often confined to a single disease, cell type or mechanism. A new collection of articles explores neurodegeneration within its physiological context, looking beyond diseased neurons to the surrounding tissue microenvironment. Research into neurodegeneration is often confined to a single disease, cell type or mechanism. This Editorial highlights a new collection of articles that explore neurodegeneration within its physiological context, looking beyond diseased neurons to the surrounding tissue microenvironment.

title: The role of small hydropower in achieving Sustainable Development Goals
content:
Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s43017-026-00843-6

The reliability and adaptability of small hydropower facilitate energy access in remote and underserved regions. This Review identifies opportunities and challenges for this technology, including environmental impacts and the increasing decarbonization of power systems, and highlights strategic interventions that optimize its sustainability and socioeconomic benefits.

title: Mangrove blue carbon in Southeast Asia
content:
Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s43017-026-00838-3

This Review examines the climate change mitigation potential of mangroves in Southeast Asia. The authors quantify emissions avoidance and restoration benefits, and discuss the socio-economic, governance and financial barriers that constrain large-scale implementation of mangrove-based blue carbon conservation and restoration.

title: Compensation of hyperexcitability with simulation-based inference
content: The activity of healthy neuronal networks is tightly regulated, and a shift toward hyperexcitability can cause various problems, such as epilepsies, memory deficits, and motor disorders. Numerous cellular, synaptic, and intrinsic mechanisms of hyperexcitability and compensatory mechanisms to restore healthy activity have been proposed. However, quantifying multiple compensatory mechanisms and their dependence on specific pathophysiological mechanisms has proven challenging, even in computational models. We use simulation-based inference to quantify the interactions of putative compensatory mechanisms in a spiking neuronal network model. Various parameters of the model can compensate for the changes in other parameters to maintain baseline activity, and we estimated their compensatory potential. Furthermore, specific causes of hyperexcitability – interneuron loss, excitatory recurrent synapses, and principal cell depolarization – have distinct compensatory mechanisms that can restore normal excitability. Our results show that spiking neuronal network simulators could generate hypotheses about the mechanisms of pathophysiological network mechanisms.

title: Distinct gradients of cortical architecture capture visual representations and behavior across the lifespan
content: The microstructure of cells within the human cerebral cortex varies across the cortical ribbon, where changes in cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture are thought to endow each region of the cortex with its unique function. While fine-scale relative to a cell, these changes at the population level impact architectural properties of the cortex measurable in vivo by noninvasive MRI, such as the thickness and myelin content of the cortex. This raises the question of whether or not we can use these in vivo architectural measures to understand cortical organization, function, and development more broadly. Using the human visual cortex as a test bed, we demonstrated two architectural gradients, one in which cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture converge and another in which they diverge. These two gradients underlie the structural and functional topography of the visual cortex, even predicting the presence of new visual representations. Moreover, the two gradients show distinct visual behavior relevance and lifespan trajectory. These findings provide a more general framework for understanding the human cortex, showing that architectural gradients are a measurable fingerprint of functional organization and ontogenetic routines in the human brain.

title: Fitness level, but not sex, affects exercise-induced pain modulation
content: In a previous study by our group (Nold et al., 2025), we investigated exercise-induced pain modulation after high-intensity compared to low-intensity exercise in a heterogeneous sample of diverse fitness levels. Exploratory analyses suggested an interaction of sex, fitness level, and drug treatment, indicating that males showed increasing hypoalgesia after high- compared to low-intensity exercise with increasing fitness levels, which was diminished when naloxone was administered. In contrast, these effects were not evident in females. These exploratory findings warranted further investigation to determine if and to what extent exercise-induced pain modulation depends on fitness level and/or sex. In this current study, we investigated an all-female sample (N=21) of high fitness levels using a similar paradigm as in the previous study, comparing heat and pressure pain ratings after high-intensity and low-intensity exercise. Our data show an interaction of exercise intensity and stimulus intensity in heat pain, with greater pain relief following high-intensity exercise, especially at the highest stimulus intensity. Despite results for pressure pain not reaching significance, a similar trend was evident. These results suggest that females at a high fitness level also show exercise-induced pain modulation for high-intensity compared to low-intensity exercise. Furthermore, we pooled the data of the current and previous study, providing evidence for fitness level but not sex to moderate exercise-induced pain modulation in heat pain. These findings suggest that exercise-induced pain modulation depends on fitness level but not on sex.

title: Glutamate receptor composition at Drosophila neuromuscular junctions depends on developmental stage and muscle identity
content: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) of larval Drosophila is widely used for studying synaptic transmission. Larval body wall muscles express five ionotropic glutamate receptor (iGluR) subunits that assemble into two tetrameric complexes, with subunit composition determining the strength and plasticity of synaptic transmission. Because NMJ function has been extensively characterized in larvae, it has commonly been assumed that adult fly NMJs share this molecular composition, despite substantial differences between life stages. Here, we systematically compare glutamate receptor expression across larval and adult Drosophila muscles. We find that adult leg and flight muscles exhibit different iGluR expression than larvae, lacking expression of several receptors previously considered essential. Adjacent muscles within the adult femur express distinct iGluRs, suggesting specialization of flexor and extensor muscles. Finally, the glutamate-gated chloride channel (GluClα) is expressed extrasynaptically in adult but not larval muscle fibers. Our results reveal unexpected heterogeneity in glutamate receptor expression across muscles and developmental stages, demonstrating the need for muscle-specific analyses in flies and other animals.

title: Oxytocin neurons signal state-dependent transitions from rest to thermogenesis and behavioral arousal
content: Core body temperature (Tb) is defended within narrow limits through thermoregulatory behaviors like huddling, nesting, and physical activity, as well as autonomic responses like brown fat thermogenesis. While Tb displays regulated fluctuations across different behavioral states and rest/arousal cycles, the neural control of these transitions remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the relationship between oxytocin neurons of the paraventricular hypothalamus (PVN<sup>OT</sup>) and behavioral and autonomic thermoeffector pathways across physiological states in mice. First, we show that PVN<sup>OT</sup> neurons are activated during social thermoregulation. We then demonstrate that in vivo PVN<sup>OT</sup> calcium dynamics align with transitions from rest to thermogenesis and behavioral arousal. Counter to our initial hypothesis, these dynamics were observed in both social and non-social contexts. Using a computer vision model to track thermoeffector pathways, we demonstrate that precisely timed stimulation of PVN<sup>OT</sup> neurons during low-Tb resting states increases thermogenesis followed by behavioral arousal. We therefore suggest a model in which PVN<sup>OT</sup> neurons facilitate homeostatic state-dependent transitions in thermo-behavioral states.

title: Evolution of Summit Magma Pressure During the 2018 Caldera Collapse at Kīlauea Volcano
content:
Abstract
We utilized geodetic data from the 16 May to 4 August 2018 caldera collapse sequence to refine the geometries and pressure evolution of two summit reservoirs at Kīlauea volcano: the shallower Halema‘uma‘u (HMM) and deeper South Caldera (SC) reservoirs. We modeled magma reservoirs as pressurized spheroidal cavities and constrained reservoir geometries with Global Positioning System (GPS) and Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar displacements. Inverting high‐rate GPS and borehole tilt time series recovered time‐dependent reservoir pressure changes and caldera ring fault shear stress. During the collapse sequence, the HMM reservoir accommodated episodic, co‐collapse pressure increases of 1.9 MPa (median) and a net 5.8 MPa (median) decrease. Simultaneously, the SC reservoir underwent monotonic depressurization of 6.7 MPa (median). Negligible co‐collapse pressure changes in the SC reservoir imply it was not exclusively supplying magma to the eruption vent. These results provide a coherent view of magma reservoir pressure evolution during the 2018 eruption.

title: Atmospheric stabilization of the East Antarctic ice sheet under warming
content:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02791-x

The long-term response of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets to warming is often studied using ice-only simulations. Here the authors use a coupled ice–atmosphere–ocean model and find that East Antarctica remains stable even under higher warming because changes in atmospheric circulation increase precipitation sensitivity.

title: Turning a Staphylococcus aureus virulence factor into an antibacterial therapy
content:
Nature Microbiology, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41564-026-02512-2

We describe FibriLysins, dual-action proteins that dismantle the fibrin structures encapsulating Staphylococcus aureus multicellular communities and kill the bacteria within. In a mouse model of device-associated infection, FibriLysins demonstrate higher antibacterial efficacy compared with the standard-of-care antibiotic vancomycin. These findings highlight the potential of FibriLysins to treat recalcitrant S. aureus infections.

title: Planetary-scale metagenomic analysis reveals CRISPR targeting dynamics across ecosystems
content:
Nature Microbiology, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41564-026-02480-7

Screening millions of CRISPR spacers across globally distributed metagenomes reveals unexpected dynamics of phage–host interactions, including many cases where phage genomes seem to repeatedly enter non-host cells.

title: A human gut-associated picobirnavirus establishes the Picobirnaviridae as the third clade of RNA bacteriophages
content:
Nature Microbiology, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41564-026-02523-z

Propagation of virions in gut-derived bacterial communities and faecal microbiota-transplanted germ-free mice establishes picobirnaviruses as a previously unknown clade of gut RNA bacteriophages.

title: Systemic exposure to typhoid toxin primes the murine vascular endothelium for intestinal perforation during Salmonella Typhi infection
content:
Nature Microbiology, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41564-026-02521-1

Typhoid toxin released during systemic infection weakens intestinal blood vessels, so that Salmonella Typhi returning to the intestine causes bleeding and lethal tissue damage in mice.

content:
